name: Pyright
summary: Microsoft’s open-source static type checker for Python, written in TypeScript, which is also the engine inside the Pylance extension for VS Code.
intro: Pyright follows the official Python typing specification and its conformance tests, and copies mypy’s behaviour where the specification is silent unless it has a reason not to. It was built to sit behind a language server: instead of checking a module top to bottom, it evaluates types lazily, working out the type of any identifier on demand, and its own parser recovers from syntax errors so it keeps working while you type. Its documentation says it is often 3 to 5 times faster than mypy on large codebases. Unannotated code is checked too, by inference. How strict it is depends on `typeCheckingMode`: `off`, `basic`, `standard` (the default since 1.1.339, December 2023) or `strict`, with every rule adjustable, set in `pyrightconfig.json` or `[tool.pyright]` in `pyproject.toml`.

The command-line tool is an npm package and needs Node.js; a community-maintained `pyright` package on PyPI installs Node for you. In VS Code, Microsoft recommends Pylance instead: a closed-source extension built on Pyright that adds features such as semantic highlighting and symbol indexing. Vim, Sublime Text and Emacs use Pyright through language-server plugins, and PyCharm has native Pyright support. basedpyright is a community fork that merges every Pyright release; version 1.1.414 shipped in September 2026.
strengths: Tracks the typing specification closely, and its documentation explains every place it differs from mypy and why
Built for editors: lazy evaluation and error-tolerant parsing keep hover, completion and diagnostics fast while you type
Checks unannotated code by inference, so it finds bugs before a codebase is fully typed
Runs in almost every editor: Pylance in VS Code, plugins for Vim, Sublime Text and Emacs, and native support in PyCharm
limits: Needs Node.js; the only official package is on npm, and the PyPI package is a community wrapper
Some editor features exist only in Pylance, which is closed source and limited to Microsoft’s VS Code (basedpyright re-implements several of them)
It must be pointed at the project’s environment: run outside it, every third-party import shows up as unresolved
Newer Rust checkers claim much higher speed: ty says 10 to 60 times faster than mypy and Pyright without caching, and Pyrefly 15 times faster on PyTorch

worksWith.how: powers the Pylance language server in

# …/shop/src/shop/orders.py:15:55 - error: Argument of type "Literal['2']" cannot be assigned
#   to parameter "id" of type "int" in function "__init__" (reportArgumentType)
# …/shop/src/shop/orders.py:16:18 - error: Type "int" is not assignable to declared type "str"
# Pydantic would quietly convert "2" to 2 at runtime; Pyright holds the model to its annotations.
# def parse(raw): return raw["id"]   adds four more errors, starting with:
# …/shop/src/shop/orders.py:20:11 - error: Type annotation is missing for parameter "raw" (reportMissingParameterType)

story: Python got standard type hints with PEP 484, but the reference checker, mypy, was designed for batch runs: it analyses modules top to bottom and relies on the interpreter’s own parser, which stops at the first syntax error. That suits CI better than an editor that has to answer “what type is this?” on every keystroke in a half-written file.

Pyright appeared on GitHub and npm in March 2019, written in TypeScript, mostly by Eric Traut, by far its largest contributor, whose GitHub profile lists Pyright among the projects worked on as a Microsoft Technical Fellow. In June 2020 Microsoft built Pylance, a new VS Code language server, on top of it, so Pyright became the type engine most VS Code Python users run without knowing its name.

In December 2023, version 1.1.339 added the `standard` mode, between `basic` and `strict`, and made it the default, covering the checks the typing standard requires. Community forks such as basedpyright followed, and from 2025 Rust-based checkers from Meta (Pyrefly) and Astral (ty) set out to beat it on speed.

choices.why: A language server needs the type of one expression now, not a full pass over the module, so Pyright evaluates only what a query depends on.
Editors are full of half-typed code; recovering from syntax errors keeps diagnostics and completion working, and newer syntax doesn’t depend on the Python version installed.
Inference gives hover types and catches bugs in code nobody has annotated yet, which matters for a tool most people meet through their editor.

choices.choice: Follow the typing spec, else mypy
choices.why: Agreeing with the spec and its conformance tests, and with mypy where the spec is silent, keeps code portable between checkers.

timeline.text: First releases on GitHub and npm, in March
1.1.339 makes the new `standard` mode the default (December)
basedpyright 1.0, a community fork, ships on PyPI
Rust-based rivals appear: Meta’s Pyrefly and Astral’s ty
